primary_claim: A prompt-optimized router that selects among trusted-editor protocols (untrusted model, gentle editor, aggressive editor, trusted coder) achieves higher usefulness than the untrusted model alone while providing 30% higher safety than the untrusted model at a 0.5% audit budget, showing that composed AI control protocols Pareto-dominate their individual components.

effect.metric: safety at 0.5% audit budget vs. untrusted model
effect.value: trained router: 30% higher safety than untrusted model while also exceeding its usefulness

contradicts_or_qualifies: Authors naively expected a linear safety-usefulness trend when randomly interpolating between trusted and untrusted policies, but observed a sub-linear trend instead
The router exceeding untrusted-model usefulness violates the usual AI control assumption that using only the untrusted model is optimal for usefulness
stated_future_work: How can safety be measured with tighter confidence intervals using fewer iterations?
How can we explain the sub-linear trend in safety-usefulness when randomly interpolating?
What other component editors should a router have access to?
Should the component editors be trained independently before training the router?
Are there red team strategies which exploit the router, e.g. by convincing it not to edit?
limitations_stated: Did not consider red-teaming strategies that explicitly target the blue team's editing and routing protocols
Training/tuning of editor and monitor could give rise to generalization issues despite using disjoint train/test sample sets, since both come from the same APPS setting
The APPS setting does not involve multi-turn interactions between red and blue team, so qualitatively new behavior could arise in more complex settings
quote: The router achieves the highest usefulness (even exceeding the untrusted model alone) while providing 30% higher safety than untrusted at 0.5% audit budget
